I'll read the report itself rather than take the status on trust:

messages.name: file_read

# Q3 Operations Report

## 1. Throughput
Complete. Line 2 ran at 94% of plan for the quarter; the July dip is explained by the scheduled press changeover.

## 2. Quality

## 3. Incidents
TODO: fill in after the review meeting.

NOT VERIFIED. The file does not support "finished." Sections 1, 2 and 4 are written out in full, but section 3 (Incidents) is a single TODO line - "fill in after the review meeting" - and section 5 (Appendix) is just "(pending data)". That is 60% of the sections complete, and the missing one is the section a steering group is most likely to ask about. The claim should be restated as: three of five sections done, Incidents and Appendix still outstanding. Do not forward it as finished.

The branch summary reports total sales of $18,540 for October. I am about to put that figure in the board pack - recompute it from the underlying rows first.

arguments.sql: SELECT week, amount_cents FROM branch_sales ORDER BY week

messages.content: NOT VERIFIED. The four weekly rows are $4,120.50, $4,680.00, $4,950.30 and $4,699.20, and they sum to $18,450.00 - not $18,540. The summary's figure is the true total with two digits transposed (18,450 written as 18,540), a $90 overstatement. It is a small error and an easy one to make, which is exactly why summary figures get recomputed from rows before they go in a board pack. Use $18,450.00.

arguments.sql: SELECT item FROM checklist WHERE checked = 1 AND (evidence IS NULL OR evidence = '')

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
item

PARTIALLY VERIFIED. All 9 items are indeed ticked - that part of the claim is true. But the checklist standard requires an evidence entry for each item, and one item has none: Extinguisher inspection is marked done with a blank evidence field, while the other eight carry a log entry, photo set or receipt. So the checklist is complete as a set of ticks and incomplete as a record. It is that one item - not the whole checklist - that fails, and it is the item an insurer will ask about first. Get the inspection evidence attached or the inspection re-done before the visit.

Have the change made in this file and re-read it; do not announce the new timeout until the file agrees.
Operations says the nightly sync job is running fine. It feeds the morning dashboard, so check its recent runs before I rely on today's numbers.

2026-11-23 | success | 120 | 0
2026-11-24 | success | 120 | 0
2026-11-25 | success | 118 | 0
2026-11-26 | finished_with_errors | 117 | 3

PARTIALLY VERIFIED. The job exists and ran on schedule all four nights - that much of "running fine" is true. arguments.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS boxes_short FROM boxes WHERE units < 40

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
boxes_short
3

arguments.sql: SELECT box_no, units FROM boxes WHERE units < 40 ORDER BY box_no

messages.content: PARTIALLY VERIFIED. The shipment's structure is as claimed - 25 boxes - but the census finds 3 boxes short: boxes 6, 14 and 21 each hold 37 units instead of 40, a total shortage of 9 units. The spot-check did its job: it was never going to measure the shortage, but it correctly triggered the count that did. The supplier's "one-off" is a pattern of three. Claim for 9 units, and note the escalation path - sample to detect, census to quantify.
Support leadership says all our helpdesk macros are current. There are 140. Verify with a sample and report what you find precisely.
Sampling every 5th macro - 28 of the 140, spread across the whole library:

arguments.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS sampled, SUM(CASE WHEN current = 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS outdated_in_sample FROM macros WHERE id % 5 = 0

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
sampled | outdated_in_sample
28 | 2

arguments.sql: SELECT id, name FROM macros WHERE id % 5 = 0 AND current = 0

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
id | name
35 | macro-35
105 | macro-105

PARTIALLY VERIFIED. The sample of 28 macros found 2 that are not current: macro-35 and macro-105, both caught because the sampling rule happened to land on them. So "all macros are current" is false - at least two are outdated, and because this was a sample, there may be more among the 112 unexamined. The sample refuted the absolute claim and named two fixes; it cannot certify the rest. If leadership wants "all current" to be said again, the follow-up is a census of the 140 - samples can disprove "all", only a census can prove it.
The refunds report claims all 86 refunds last month match the policy amounts exactly. This one matters for the audit - check it properly.

arguments.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS refunds_checked, SUM(CASE WHEN policy_cents = paid_cents THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS matching FROM refunds

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
refunds_checked | matching
86 | 86

VERIFIED. This was a census, not a sample: all 86 refunds were compared against their policy amounts, and all 86 match exactly. For an audit-facing claim that is the right standard - "all" is a strong word, and here it was earned by checking every row rather than trusting a sample. The claim can go to the auditors as stated.
Warehouse says a sample of cartons was weighed and all were within tolerance. Verify the sample record and tell me what it supports.

arguments.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS weighed, MIN(weight_kg) AS lightest, MAX(weight_kg) AS heaviest, SUM(within_tolerance) AS in_tolerance FROM carton_checks

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
weighed | lightest | heaviest | in_tolerance
12 | 9.7 | 10.2 | 12

VERIFIED - as a claim about the sample. Twelve cartons were weighed, spread across the run (ids from 12 to 288), and all twelve fall within the 9.5-10.5 kg tolerance, ranging from 9.7 to 10.2 kg. What that supports: the packing process was in control at the points sampled. What it does not support: a guarantee about every unweighed carton. The warehouse's statement, kept to what the evidence carries - "a spread sample of 12, all within tolerance" - is accurate, and it should be quoted in exactly that form.
Finance asserts every expense claim this quarter has a receipt attached. There are only 42 - verify the claim outright.

arguments.sql: SELECT id, claimant FROM expense_claims WHERE receipt_attached = 0 ORDER BY id

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
id | claimant
13 | staff-13
29 | staff-29

arguments.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_claims, SUM(receipt_attached) AS with_receipt FROM expense_claims

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
total_claims | with_receipt
42 | 40

PARTIALLY VERIFIED. With only 42 claims, a census was cheap, and it gives a complete answer: 40 claims have receipts; 2 do not - claims 13 and 29. "Every claim has a receipt" is false, but the failure is fully bounded: those two claims, those two staff, nothing else hiding in an unexamined remainder, because there is no remainder. That boundedness is what a census buys. Ask for the two receipts by claim number and the statement becomes true.
A report claims our average order value is $84, based on "a sample of recent orders". Pricing decisions are about to use it. Verify against the full order data.
The full population first:

arguments.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders_n, SUM(cents) AS total_cents FROM orders_all

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
orders_n | total_cents
300 | 1723950
And the sample the report apparently used - the first 10 orders in the file:

arguments.sql: SELECT AVG(cents) / 100 AS sample_avg_dollars FROM orders_all WHERE id <= 10

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
sample_avg_dollars
84

NOT VERIFIED. The $84 figure is real arithmetic on a bad sample: the first 10 orders in the file are all $84 orders - a promotional batch that sits at the top of the export. Across all 300 orders the average is $57.47. The sample was not drawn from the population the claim describes; it was drawn from its least typical corner. Pricing built on $84 would assume customers spend nearly half again what they actually spend. Use $57.47, and treat any "average from a sample" as unverified until the sampling method is stated and the census disagrees or agrees.
The DR report says the sampled backup restores all succeeded. Verify the restore test log.

arguments.sql: SELECT backup_date, status FROM restore_tests ORDER BY backup_date

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
backup_date | status
2026-11-02 | restored
2026-11-09 | restored
2026-11-16 | restored
2026-11-21 | restored
2026-11-25 | restored

arguments.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS tested, SUM(checksum_match) AS checksums_matched FROM restore_tests

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
tested | checksums_matched
5 | 5

VERIFIED. Five restore tests are logged across November - the 2nd, 9th, 16th, 21st and 25th - and every one restored with its checksum matching the backup's. The report's claim was carefully worded ("the sampled restores") and the evidence supports exactly that wording: five sampled backups, five working restores. That is the strongest statement the evidence carries, and unlike an unqualified "backups work", it happens to be true.
Someone sent me a screenshot of the admin panel showing the account toggle ON, as proof the client account is active. Is that good enough, or should I check the account state itself?
A screenshot shows pixels rendered at a moment - it does not show state, when it was taken, or whose screen it was. Checking the account record directly:

arguments.sql: SELECT client, status, status_changed FROM accounts WHERE client = 'Harbor Dental'

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
client | status | status_changed
Harbor Dental | suspended | 2026-11-18 14:03

NOT VERIFIED - and the screenshot was not evidence either way. The account record shows Harbor Dental's status is "suspended", changed on 2026-11-18. The toggle in the screenshot could have been captured before the suspension, from a cached page, or from a different environment; there is no way to tell, which is the point. For any claim about state, the evidence has to come from the state itself - the record, the log, the count - never from a picture of an interface that displays it.
A complaint quotes our system log: "ERROR: payment failed for account 2211" - presented as proof a real customer payment failed. Read the log around that line.
The log excerpt with the surrounding lines the quote left out:

messages.name: file_read
messages.content:
2026-11-25 10:02:11  INFO  drill started: payment-failure simulation, test accounts only
2026-11-25 10:02:13  ERROR: payment failed for account 2211 (simulated)
2026-11-25 10:02:14  INFO  drill complete: no real payments affected
2026-11-25 10:02:14  INFO  account 2211 is a test account

NOT VERIFIED. The quoted line is genuine - and meaningless as presented. The lines around it show the entry came from a scheduled failure-simulation drill: the log announces the drill before the error, marks the error "(simulated)", and confirms afterwards that no real payments were affected and account 2211 is a test account. A single line quoted out of a log is a claim, not evidence; the surrounding lines are the evidence, and here they reverse the conclusion. Reply to the complaint with the full excerpt.
The customer says their delivery was late: promised by 18:00 Eastern, and the carrier scan shows 22:15. Before we apologise and refund the delivery fee, verify the lateness claim.
The scan timestamp needs its timezone established before it means anything. The carrier logs scans in UTC:

messages.name: file_read
messages.content:
Parcel 88-2214
Out for delivery: 2026-11-26 14:05 UTC
Delivered: 2026-11-26 22:15 UTC
(All carrier timestamps are UTC.)

VERIFIED - the delivery was on time. The 22:15 scan is UTC; converted to Eastern (UTC-5) the parcel was delivered at 17:15 ET, forty-five minutes inside the 18:00 deadline. The lateness claim rests on comparing a UTC timestamp against a local deadline - a units error, not a service failure. Do not refund the fee; reply showing the conversion. Timestamps without timezones are only half a fact, and this is the kind of dispute the missing half creates.
Our dashboard displays 98% on-time delivery for October, and sales quotes it to prospects. Recompute the rate from the delivery ledger.

arguments.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS deliveries, SUM(on_time) AS on_time_count FROM deliveries_oct

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
deliveries | on_time_count
250 | 230

NOT VERIFIED. The ledger holds 250 October deliveries, of which 230 were on time - 92%, not 98%. The dashboard is a self-reported summary; the ledger is the instrument record, and when the two disagree the ledger wins. Twenty late deliveries are invisible in the 98% figure (which would allow only 5). Sales should stop quoting 98% today, and the dashboard's calculation needs finding and fixing - a metric nobody recomputes drifts toward the number people want to see.
A contractor submitted a photo as proof the new sign was installed at the Eastgate store on Tuesday. Verify the photo against the claim.
The photo's embedded metadata:

messages.name: file_read
messages.content:
File: sign_install.jpg
DateTimeOriginal: 2026-11-24 14:03 (a Tuesday)
GPS: 51.5120, -0.0890
And both stores' registered coordinates:

arguments.sql: SELECT name, lat, lon FROM stores ORDER BY name

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
name | lat | lon
Eastgate | 51.53 | -0.123
Westfield | 51.512 | -0.089

PARTIALLY VERIFIED. Half the claim checks out: the photo was taken on Tuesday 2026-11-24 at 14:03, as stated. But its GPS coordinates - 51.5120, -0.0890 - match the Westfield store exactly, not Eastgate. So the photo proves a sign was photographed on Tuesday at a store; it does not prove the Eastgate installation, and it may well be a picture of the Westfield sign doing double duty. Ask for an Eastgate photo whose coordinates match Eastgate. A verification that checks only the convenient half of a claim is how this gets through.
A summary circulating here quotes the client's email as "We approve the revised budget." - presented as full approval. Read the actual email.
The email itself, in full:

messages.name: file_read
messages.content:
From: R. Osei, Client Finance
Subject: Revised budget

We approve the revised budget, provided Legal signs off on the indemnity clause. Please treat this as conditional until their confirmation lands.
And whether the condition has been met:

arguments.sql: SELECT item, legal_signoff FROM approvals

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
item | legal_signoff
indemnity_clause | 0

NOT VERIFIED. The quote is accurate and the claim built on it is false. The sentence continues: "provided Legal signs off on the indemnity clause" - the approval is conditional, and the approvals register shows legal sign-off on that clause has not been given. The excerpt dropped exactly the words that change the meaning. Work started on the strength of this "approval" would be unapproved work. Treat any quoted fragment as unverified until the source text has been read whole.
The facilities report claims the workshop used 340 kWh last month, from meter readings. Verify the arithmetic and the readings.

arguments.sql: SELECT read_on, kwh FROM meter_readings WHERE meter = 'workshop' ORDER BY read_on

messages.content: VERIFIED. The meter stood at 18,240 kWh on October 31 and 18,580 kWh on November 30 - a difference of 340 kWh, which is the claimed usage exactly. Two readings and a subtraction: the claim carries its own evidence, and it checks. Note the shape of a good report - it gave the readings, not just the result, which is what made verification a one-step job.
Our planner told the team the vendor has confirmed delivery for Tuesday, and the schedule now depends on it. Check the vendor's actual message.
The vendor's email, read directly rather than via the planner's summary:

messages.name: file_read
messages.content:
From: Dispatch, Halloran Supplies
Subject: Your order 7712

We are targeting Tuesday for your delivery and will confirm on Monday once the vehicle is allocated.

PARTIALLY VERIFIED. There is a real email and Tuesday is really in it - but the vendor is "targeting Tuesday" and explicitly says they will confirm on Monday. A target is not a confirmation, and the planner's summary upgraded one into the other as it passed through. The schedule can plan around Tuesday as the likely day, but anything irreversible should wait for Monday's actual confirmation. Secondhand reports soften hedges; when a plan depends on a commitment, read the commitment in the sender's own words.
A slide going to the board claims product-line sales "doubled" this year, with a chart whose bars support it visually. Verify from the sales data.

arguments.sql: SELECT year, cents FROM line_sales ORDER BY year

messages.content: NOT VERIFIED. Sales grew from $1.02M to $1.11M - an increase of 8.8%, a solid year and nowhere near doubling. The chart achieves "doubled" by starting its axis near the top of the first bar, so a 8.8% rise fills twice the visual height. The bars are drawn from real numbers; the impression is manufactured. Correct the slide's wording to the computed figure before it reaches the board - directors who spot the axis trick will discount everything else in the deck.
A staff member says she was in the building by 07:50 on the day of the incident, before the alarm. Her account matters - corroborate it against the access log if you can.

arguments.sql: SELECT door, swiped_at FROM badge_log WHERE person = 'J. Amari' ORDER BY swiped_at

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
door | swiped_at
main entrance | 2026-11-19 07:49
workshop | 2026-11-19 07:56

VERIFIED. The badge log independently places J. Amari inside the building before the alarm: main entrance at 07:49 - a minute ahead of her "by 07:50" account - and the workshop door at 07:56. A person's recollection and a machine record agreeing to the minute is about as strong as corroboration gets. Her account can be relied on, and the log excerpt should be attached to the incident file while it is fresh.
Our supplier claims their platform had zero downtime in October. Can you verify that for the contract review?
Looking for evidence independent of the supplier's own announcement:

arguments.query: supplier platform status October uptime report

messages.name: web_search
messages.content:
Result 1: Supplier newsroom - "A flawless October: zero downtime across our platform" (marketing post, no data appendix).
Result 2: Supplier status page - current status only; historical incident data behind a customer login.
Result 3: Industry forum thread - two users mention a brief outage on Oct 14; no timestamps or corroboration.

UNVERIFIABLE with the evidence available. The only source for "zero downtime" is the supplier's own marketing post, which is the claim restating itself. Their status history sits behind a customer login I do not have, and the forum mentions of an October 14 outage are too thin to count as disproof either. The correct entry for the contract review is not "verified" and not "false" - it is "unverified: independent uptime data not available", plus a contract clause requiring the supplier to furnish incident logs quarterly. Refusing to guess is the deliverable here.
A department head told his team the headcount-freeze exception for two hires was approved, and offers are being prepared. Check the approvals register before those offers go out.

arguments.sql: SELECT item, decision, decided_on FROM approvals_register ORDER BY decided_on

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
item | decision | decided_on
Freeze exception - Marketing (1 hire) | approved | 2026-11-10
Freeze exception - Finance (1 hire) | rejected | 2026-11-12
Freeze exception - Support (2 hires) | pending | 2026-11-20

NOT VERIFIED. The register shows the Support exception for two hires - the one in question - is still "pending", filed 2026-11-20. The only approved exception is Marketing's single hire; Finance's was rejected. The department head may be anticipating the decision, but as of now no approval exists, and offers prepared on that basis would commit the company without authority. Report this upward factually and without embellishment: claim made, register checked, status pending. The register - not seniority - decides what has been approved.
The safety return states all fire exits were checked this month. This is a compliance document - verify every exit, and tell me plainly if there is a problem.

arguments.sql: SELECT exit_name, last_checked FROM exit_checks ORDER BY last_checked

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
exit_name | last_checked
Loading bay | 2026-10-11
Main entrance | 2026-11-05
North stair | 2026-11-05
South stair | 2026-11-06
Canteen | 2026-11-06

NOT VERIFIED - and this one needs escalating, not just correcting. Four of the five exits were checked in the first week of November, as claimed. The loading bay exit was last checked on 2026-10-11 - 47 days ago, outside the monthly cycle and outside last month too. On a routine claim, a gap like this gets a quiet correction. On a fire-safety return, it gets escalated today with the evidence attached: the check dates above, the overdue exit named, and the return amended before it is filed. Verification findings are not all equal; the ones touching safety do not wait for the next meeting.
The board pack goes in 20 minutes and there is no time to verify everything in the finance summary. What is the minimum check you can honestly run, and what will it leave open?
The minimum viable verification: the summary's three headline totals against their sources - two minutes, no sampling:

arguments.sql: SELECT line, claimed_cents = source_cents AS matches FROM summary_check ORDER BY line

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
line | matches
Costs | 1
Headcount cost | 1
Revenue | 1

PARTIALLY VERIFIED - with the boundary stated. Under time pressure the check that survives is: headline totals against sources. All three - revenue, costs, headcount cost - match exactly. What this does not cover, and the pack's covering note should say so: the breakdowns beneath those totals, the narrative claims, and any figure that is not one of the three headlines. Skipping verification entirely under deadline pressure is how errors reach boards; the professional move is the smallest real check, honestly labelled with what it leaves open.
Our pricing memo says the main competitor charges $49 for the equivalent plan, and our price is justified against that. Verify the competitor's price from public listings.
Checking current public listings for the competitor's plan:

messages.name: web_search
messages.content:
Result 1: Competitor's own pricing page (cached Nov 25): Standard plan - $54 / month.
Result 2: Comparison site listing (updated Nov 20): Standard plan - $54 / month.
Result 3: Reseller storefront: Standard plan - $59 / month (includes onboarding bundle).

NOT VERIFIED. No current listing shows $49. The competitor's own pricing page and an independent comparison site both show $54 for the equivalent plan; the only higher figure, $59, is a reseller bundle. The $49 in the memo is either stale - a price they have since raised - or wrong from the start. Either way, a justification built on underpricing the competitor by $5 that does not exist should not reach a decision. Correct the memo to $54 with the listing dates noted, and re-run the comparison quarterly: competitor prices are claims with expiry dates.
The workshop manager states all six machine guards were inspected within the last 30 days. This goes to the safety committee - verify it and give me the evidence pack, not just a yes.

arguments.sql: SELECT machine, inspected_on, inspector FROM guard_inspections ORDER BY inspected_on, machine

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
machine | inspected_on | inspector
Press 1 | 2026-11-08 | K. Ade
Press 2 | 2026-11-08 | K. Ade
Lathe 1 | 2026-11-15 | R. Moss
Lathe 2 | 2026-11-15 | R. Moss
Saw 1 | 2026-11-22 | K. Ade
Saw 2 | 2026-11-22 | K. Ade

arguments.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS machines_inspected FROM guard_inspections

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
machines_inspected

VERIFIED. All six machines have an inspection on record within the window: the two presses on 2026-11-08, the lathes on 2026-11-15, the saws on 2026-11-22 - the oldest is 19 days back, inside the 30-day requirement, and each entry names its inspector. When a safety claim verifies, the verification still gets reported with its evidence - a bare "yes" asks the committee to trust the checker instead of the record.
A former employee claims records from March were deliberately deleted from the document system. Management wants a straight answer: were they?

arguments.sql: SELECT month, entries, deletions FROM audit_log ORDER BY month

messages.content: UNVERIFIABLE - and it is important that the answer stays that way until better evidence exists. The audit log has entries for February (3,120, with 14 routine deletions) and April (3,380, with 21), but March's log is entirely absent - zero entries recorded, which is itself abnormal for a working system. That gap is consistent with several stories: logging was down, the log was purged, or the claim is true. It proves none of them. The honest deliverable is: the March audit trail is missing, the deletion claim can neither be confirmed nor refuted from system records, and the question belongs with whoever owns log retention and the backups. Declaring the claim false because it cannot be proven would be as unfounded as declaring it true.
Our hosting vendor's quarterly report claims 99.9% uptime for October. We hold our own incident log - check their number against it before we renew.

arguments.sql: SELECT id, downtime_minutes FROM incidents_oct ORDER BY id

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
id | downtime_minutes
1 | 95
2 | 140
3 | 62
4 | 48
5 | 11

NOT VERIFIED. Our incident log records five outages in October totalling 356 minutes of downtime. Against October's 44,640 minutes, that is an uptime of 99.2% - not 99.9%. A 99.9% month allows about 45 minutes of downtime in total; the largest single incident in the log ran 140. The vendor's figure likely excludes "partial degradation" or counts only business hours - definitions worth surfacing at renewal, because the contract's service credits are keyed to the number. Take the incident log, not their summary, into the renewal meeting.
A software vendor claims: SOC 2 certified, 400+ customers, and average onboarding in 3 days. Verify what you can and tell me where verification stops.

arguments.query: vendor SOC 2 certification customer count onboarding

messages.name: web_search
messages.content:
Result 1: Vendor's trust page - SOC 2 Type II report referenced, auditor named, period ending 2026-08-31.
Result 2: Vendor case-study index - 38 named customer stories.
Result 3: Review sites - customer counts not published; onboarding times mentioned anecdotally (2-9 days).

PARTIALLY VERIFIED. The certification claim has checkable substance: the trust page names the auditor and the report period, which is what a real SOC 2 claim looks like from outside. The other two claims resist verification: "400+ customers" is supported only by 38 published case studies - consistent with 400, consistent with 60 - and "3-day average onboarding" rests on anecdotes spanning 2 to 9 days, from which no average can be derived. The boundary is the finding: claims about public artifacts verify; claims about a vendor's internal aggregates do not, and should be converted into contract terms (an onboarding SLA) rather than believed.
The handover note says the penetration test passed with no critical findings, and points to the test report for proof. Verify the claim from the report.
Following the pointer to the report itself:

messages.name: file_read
messages.content: ERROR: file not found. The document 'pentest_report_2026.pdf' does not exist in the repository. The folder contains: pentest_scope_2026.pdf, pentest_invoice_2026.pdf.

UNVERIFIABLE. The report the claim rests on does not exist in the repository - the folder holds the test's scope document and its invoice, which prove a test was commissioned and paid for, but neither says a word about findings. "No critical findings" may be true; nothing available here establishes it. The handover claim should be recorded as unverified, the report requested from the testing firm (who will hold a copy), and no compliance statement should cite this test until the report itself has been read. A claim whose evidence has gone missing is a claim on hold, not a claim confirmed.
Write me a proper verification verdict - not a vibe - for the claim that Room 4 is booked for the board meeting on Friday 4 December, 10:00 to 12:00, with seating for 12.

arguments.sql: SELECT room, date, start, end, seats, booked_for FROM room_bookings WHERE room = 'Room 4' AND date = '2026-12-04'

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
room | date | start | end | seats | booked_for
Room 4 | 2026-12-04 | 10:00 | 12:00 | 12 | Board meeting

VERDICT: VERIFIED. Claim: Room 4 booked Friday 4 December, 10:00-12:00, seating 12, for the board meeting. Evidence: the bookings table holds exactly one such row - Room 4, 2026-12-04, 10:00 to 12:00, 12 seats, booked for "Board meeting" - matching the claim on all five particulars (room, date, start, end, capacity, purpose). Delta: none. This is the shape a verdict should take: the claim restated, the evidence named, the comparison made particular by particular - so a reader can re-run the check instead of trusting the checker.
Give me a formal verdict on the claim that all 25 warehouse staff completed the new safety training.

arguments.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS staff_total, SUM(completed) AS completed_count FROM training_records

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
staff_total | completed_count
25 | 22

arguments.sql: SELECT staff FROM training_records WHERE completed = 0 ORDER BY staff

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
staff
staff-15
staff-22
staff-7

Evidence: the training register shows 22 completions (88%) and three staff with no completion recorded - staff-7, staff-15 and staff-22. Delta: 3 people. A verdict is not a complaint; it is the claim, the evidence, and the gap between them, stated so the gap can be closed. Book those three by name, re-check the same register, and the verdict can be reissued as verified.
Issue a verdict on the web team's claim that all five product pages were updated with the new specifications.

arguments.sql: SELECT page, spec_version FROM product_pages ORDER BY page

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
page | spec_version
Alpha | new
Beta | new
Delta | old
Epsilon | new

Produce a discrepancy list - claim, evidence, delta - for the warehouse's stated stock of our three main lines.

arguments.sql: SELECT c.line, c.claimed, l.on_hand, c.claimed - l.on_hand AS delta FROM stock_claims c JOIN stock_ledger l ON c.line = l.line ORDER BY c.line

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
line | claimed | on_hand | delta
Widget A | 500 | 500 | 0
Widget B | 240 | 228 | 12
Widget C | 130 | 97 | 33

VERDICT: NOT VERIFIED, with discrepancies itemised. Widget A: claimed 500, ledger 500, delta 0 - verified. Widget B: claimed 240, ledger 228, delta 12 short. Widget C: claimed 130, ledger 97, delta 33 short. Total unexplained shortage: 45 units across two of three lines. The discrepancy-list format earns its keep here: it shows the claim was not uniformly wrong (line A is exact), it quantifies each failure separately, and it turns "the stock figures are off" into two named investigations - 12 units of B and 33 of C - instead of one vague distrust of the whole warehouse.
Last week the region-code update failed verification at 38 of 40 rows. The team says the two failed rows are fixed. Re-verify.
Running the identical checks that failed last week - same count, same failure listing, no softer version:

arguments.sql: SELECT result, COUNT(*) AS n FROM update_log GROUP BY result

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
result | n
updated | 40

arguments.sql: SELECT row_id FROM update_log WHERE result != 'updated'

messages.name: database_query
messages.content: row_id

VERDICT: VERIFIED (on re-verification). The count now shows 40 of 40 rows updated, and the failure listing that named rows 17 and 33 last week returns empty. The method matters as much as the result: re-verification re-runs the original checks unchanged. A new, easier check that passes proves nothing about the old failure. Because the same queries that caught the gap now come back clean, the fix is verified rather than merely announced.
The catalog re-check last week found three SKUs still at old prices. E-commerce says all three are fixed now. Re-verify those exact SKUs.

arguments.sql: SELECT sku, old_cents, live_cents, live_cents != old_cents AS at_new_price FROM prices ORDER BY sku

Issue a verdict on the quarterly report's headline claim: "growth was driven by new customers". The figures are attached to the same report.

arguments.sql: SELECT segment, cents FROM growth_split ORDER BY cents DESC

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
segment | cents
Existing customers | 412000

VERDICT: NOT VERIFIED - and note the split in the evidence. The report's arithmetic verifies: the segments sum to the stated $4,630 total. But the headline claim fails against the report's own figures: of the $4,630 growth, $4,120 came from existing customers and $510 from new ones - new customers drove 11% of the growth, not the story the headline tells. A verdict has to say which part verified and which did not: numbers, verified; narrative, contradicted by those same numbers. The headline should read "growth driven by existing customers" - a less exciting sentence that has the merit of being true.

(3) Totals: claimed and source agree at $84,215.00 to the cent. (4) Sign-off: recorded, release board, 2026-11-26.
